b: This is the most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient countries and the most common thyroid disease overall . It involves autoimmune destruction of the thyroid, with associated antibodies being anti-thyroid peroxidase (Anti-T
Pathogenesis: Primarily mediated by CD8+ cytotoxic T cells, with autoantibodies also playing a role.
Histology: Dense lymphocytic infiltration with germinal centers, Hürthle cell change (large pink cells), follicular atrophy, and fibrosis.
Clinical course: Can present with transient hyperthyroidism ("Hashitoxicosis") followed by hypothyroidism. The thyroid is typically firm and rubbery.
Complications: Increased risk of thyroid lymphoma and papillary thyroid carcinoma.

qs.q: A patient with Hashimoto's thyroiditis typically exhibits which of the following histological features?
o: Dense lymphocytic infiltration with germinal centers and Hürthle cell change
Psammoma bodies and overlapping nuclei with prominent nuclear grooves
Follicular hyperplasia with scalloped colloid and crowded epithelial cells
Granulomatous inflammation with multinucleated giant cells and central necrosis
qs.e: Hashimoto's thyroiditis is characterized histologically by a dense lymphoplasmacytic infiltration with germinal centers and Hürthle cell metaplasia. Granulomatous inflammation with giant cells is instead seen in De Quervain's subacute thyroiditis.

qs.q: Which underlying mechanism is responsible for autoimmune-mediated hypothyroidism in Hashimoto’s thyroiditis?
o: Hyperstimulation of pituitary TSH receptors
Immune-mediated destruction of thyroid tissue
Overactivity of intracellular deiodinases
Excessive dietary iodine supplementation
qs.e: Hashimoto’s thyroiditis leads to immune-mediated destruction of thyroid tissue, resulting in decreased hormone output and clinical hypothyroidism. Dietary iodine deficiency is a distinct, non-autoimmune cause of hypothyroidism.

qs.q: Hashimoto's thyroiditis is associated with antibodies against ---
o: B. Antibodies to T3 and T4 hormones
C. Antibodies to thyroglobulin and thyroid peroxidase
D. Antibodies to thyroid‑stimulating immunoglobulins
A. Antibodies to TSH receptor
qs.e: Hashimoto's thyroiditis is characterized by anti‑thyroglobulin and anti‑thyroid peroxidase antibodies.

o: Follicular hyperplasia with scalloped colloid and absent lymphocytes
Granulomatous inflammation with giant cells and fibrosis
Psammoma bodies and papillary architecture
Dense lymphocytic infiltration with germinal centers and Hürthle cell change
qs.e: Lymphoplasmacytic infiltration + Hürthle cell metaplasia. Anti-TPO antibodies elevated. Most common cause of hypothyroidism in iodine-sufficient regions.

exam: A 35‑year‑old woman from a rural clinic presents with a painless goitre and TSH 12 mIU/L. What is the next step? — Check anti‑TPO antibodies; if positive, start levothyroxine and arrange follow‑up.

During a ward round you note a patient with known Hashimoto now has a rapidly enlarging thyroid and dysphagia. What must you consider? — Possible thyroid lymphoma; order urgent ultrasound and refer for fine‑needle aspiration.
A patient with Hashimoto is on levothyroxine but complains of palpitations and tremor. What is the most likely cause? — Overtreatment (excess dose); check free T4 and reduce levothyroxine dose.

How does Hashitoxicosis differ from Graves disease in terms of antibodies? — Hashitoxicosis lacks TSH‑receptor antibodies; Hashimoto shows anti‑TPO/thyroglobulin, while Graves has stimulating TSH‑R antibodies.
Why should calcium supplements be taken separately from levothyroxine? — Calcium chelates levothyroxine, reducing absorption and risking under‑replacement.

In a low‑resource hospital without ultrasound, how would you monitor for thyroid lymphoma? — Rely on clinical signs (rapid growth, compressive symptoms) and repeat physical exams; refer for imaging when available.
What is the rationale for avoiding iodine‑rich herbal remedies in a patient with Hashimoto? — Excess iodine can trigger or worsen autoimmune thyroiditis, accelerating hypothyroidism.

A patient with hypothyroidism on levothyroxine presents with cold intolerance but normal TSH. What should you assess? — Adherence, timing of medication, interfering drugs (e.g., iron), and possible malabsorption.
ai.title: Hashimoto Thyroiditis
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Hashimoto thyroiditis is chronic autoimmune thyroiditis, the leading cause of hypothyroidism in iodine‑sufficient regions. It presents with a firm, rubbery gland, variable thyroid function and risk of lymphoma.

b: Elevated anti‑thyroid peroxidase (anti‑TPO) or anti‑thyroglobulin antibodies
TSH > 4.5 mIU/L with low free T4 confirms hypothyroidism; low TSH with high free T4 suggests transient Hashitoxicosis
sections.p: An immune‑mediated destruction of thyroid follicles that leads to progressive loss of hormone production. Diagnosis rests on clinical features, thyroid function tests and auto‑antibodies.

b: Subclinical hypothyroidism: TSH 4.5‑10 mIU/L, normal free T4
Overt hypothyroidism: TSH >10 mIU/L, low free T4
Hashitoxicosis: suppressed TSH, elevated free T4/T3, usually self‑limited
sections.p: Severity is gauged by thyroid function and gland morphology rather than a formal stage system.

b: Genetic predisposition (HLA‑DR5, CTLA‑4)
Iodine excess (common where iodised salt is newly introduced)
Infections: HIV, hepatitis C, TB (immune activation)
Herbal or traditional remedies containing goitrogens
sections.p: Autoimmune dysregulation is primary; several environmental triggers are recognised, especially in low‑resource settings.

b: Painless, firm, rubbery thyroid enlargement
Fatigue, weight gain, cold intolerance (hypothyroid)
Palpitations, heat intolerance early on (Hashitoxicosis)
Dry skin, hair loss, menstrual irregularities
sections.p: Patients may be asymptomatic, have a painless goitre, or show fluctuating thyroid function.
When a test is unavailable, rely on clinical picture and basic labs (TSH, free T4, antibodies) and refer for imaging if possible.

t.b: Is the thyroid under‑ or over‑active? High TSH/low free T4 = hypothyroidism; low TSH/high free T4 = Hashitoxicosis
Do auto‑antibodies support an autoimmune cause? Positive titres strongly suggest Hashimoto
What is gland morphology? Heterogeneous echotexture, hypoechoic areas, possible nodules; guides need for fine‑needle aspiration
Is there malignancy? Cytology distinguishes lymphoma or papillary carcinoma from benign Hashimoto changes
Is excess iodine contributing? High urinary iodine may support iodine‑induced acceleration

b: Rapid neck swelling, dysphagia or hoarseness → possible thyroid lymphoma
New cervical lymphadenopathy → consider malignancy
Myxedema coma in untreated severe hypothyroidism (altered mental status, hypothermia, hypotension)
sections.p: Complications are usually delayed but can become urgent.

b: Levothyroxine replacement (synthetic T4) – restores euthyroidism; preferred over combination therapy because of predictable absorption
Avoid iodine excess (iodised salt in excess, kelp supplements) which can worsen autoimmunity
If Hashitoxicosis, provide β‑blocker for symptomatic tachycardia; avoid antithyroid drugs as the phase is self‑limited
Surveillance for lymphoma: repeat ultrasound if gland enlarges rapidly or symptoms change
sections.p: Treat the hormone deficit, monitor for complications, and avoid unnecessary interventions.

b: TSH and free T4 every 6‑12 months after starting levothyroxine; more often if dose changes
Anti‑TPO titres are not needed for routine follow‑up but may be checked if diagnosis is uncertain
Educate patients on consistent levothyroxine intake (empty stomach, separate from calcium/iron)
Counsel on avoiding excess iodine and unnecessary herbal supplements
sections.p: Long‑term monitoring is essential because disease course can change.

b: Subacute (de Quervain) thyroiditis – painful, viral, transient hyperthyroidism, elevated ESR
Graves disease – diffuse goitre, ophthalmopathy, persistent hyperthyroidism, TSH‑receptor antibodies
Normal anti‑TPO does not exclude early Hashimoto; rely on clinical picture and repeat testing
Transiently low TSH during Hashitoxicosis may be misread as Graves disease; absence of TSH‑receptor antibodies and painful thyroid help differentiate

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden neck swelling with airway compromise
Signs of myxedema coma (altered consciousness, hypothermia, hypotension)
Rapidly enlarging thyroid with systemic B symptoms (fever, night sweats, weight loss)
